To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
secondary pupils have relatively rich experiences and perceptions of the nature of research, and that their experiences and perceptions of it vary considerably across different disciplines.

(i) pupils’ experiences and conceptions of research are relatively rich; (ii) pupils are more likely to have positive perceptions of research in the context of science and humanities subjects than in the context of mathematics, and in the context of their own research than in the context in which they have been exposed to research; (iii) pupils’ conceptions of research tend to be limited in scope and depth, and are often inconsistent; (iv) pupils tend to perceive research as fact-finding
secondary pupils’ perceptions of research vary across disciplines and that they could benefit from more comprehensive engagement.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the question: how might we best engage pupils with research in the secondary classroom, and what might be the consequences of doing so?
how pupils’ perceptions of research might be enhanced through their engagement in research processes.
the extent to which the school system in England is preparing pupils to engage in research as a way of knowing, and we suggest that it is not.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the research process and its utility and significance are poorly understood and appreciated by many secondary school pupils.
pupils’ experiences and understanding of research are limited, and that they are often unaware of the research process.

pupils’ experiences of research and their perceptions of what research is and what it is for are varied and, in many cases, underdeveloped, but there are many positive examples of pupils engaging with research processes.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

pupils’ perceptions of research are not as simplistic as is sometimes supposed and that pupils’ engagement with research processes can be enhanced through the provision of more opportunities and more support.
pupils’ perceptions of research are not as narrow or as simplistic as is sometimes suggested.
pupils are more likely to be engaged with research if they are able to understand it as a process, not as an end product.
The main takeaway from our work is that
pupils’ engagement with research should not be seen as a luxury, but a necessity if they are to become informed and engaged citizens and lifelong learners.
pupils need to experience research as something they can do themselves and that they can do well.
pupils’ perceptions of research are not as negative as is commonly thought.
